title: Ignite 2026: Building the frontier ecosystem
body: Ignite 2026: Building the frontier ecosystem Nov 17, 2026 | Microsoft Corporate Blogs Satya Nadella, Microsoft Chairman and CEO, delivered the opening keynote at Ignite in San Francisco this morning. Here is an edited version of his remarks. This week is about two things: First is how we capitalize on new capabilities that are growing exponentially. And second is how do we build the capability to deal with the consequences of these exponentials. At times like these, I always find it helpful to be grounded in our mission: To empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. In today’s world, that means building a frontier ecosystem. We need to parlay any technological advance into real outcomes and new points of leverage for people, organizations and society at large. For us, that comes down to three things: Keeping human ambition at the center, ensuring your control of your organization’s intelligence and learning, and trust. And so, our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three core architectural principles. Copilot Copilot is the new OS for work . Copilot brings together all the new form factors of human-computer interaction, whether it is Chat, Cowork, Code or Autopilot, into one experience. It also brings together the disparate categories of knowledge work, coding and business process. That is why we have all of Office with its richness built into Copilot. And underlying it is a model system that matches the right intelligence to the right context to the right form factor to accomplish the task. Home gives you one place to start, whether you need a quick answer or want to assign and complete complex, multi-step tasks. Code brings the power of an infinite SaaS factory to every individual. It lets you build your own custom SaaS apps, dashboards and much more. And Autopilot is an autonomous agent that keeps moving your work forward 24×7 in all the places where you and your team collaborate. Underlying all this is Work IQ. You can think of this as the most important database for any organization, with a deep understanding of people, their relationships, documents, emails, meetings, chats and projects that make up the fabric of work. And we are going further. We are extending Copilot for specific roles: sales, legal, finance, service. We are organizing the skills, connectors and plugins for these roles across the entire surface area of Copilot. And that includes third-party systems, too. In fact, today we are announcing new plugins for business applications, starting with Dynamics 365. And it is not just Dynamics. We are very excited to partner with Salesforce to bring Salesforce to Copilot . And we are going beyond that as well. Up until now, we have mostly been in a single player world of people and their agent loops and swarms. But the time has come for a true multiplayer form factor, where people, their agents and other people are all driving towards a common goal, with shared context. This is Copilot Workspaces: YouTube Video Click here to load media Microsoft IQ The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain and continuously improve its own intelligence. Essentially, we are taking the system we built underneath Copilot and externalizing it as a first-class platform that embodies your organizational intelligence as an asset that you continuously build and control. We are bringing together all of the data you have across Fabric, Foundry and Microsoft 365. And, of course, all the third-party context too. Microsoft IQ comes with hundreds of new connectors we are announcing today, so agents can get the full enterprise context where business gets done. And all this rich context manifests as business plugins that can be shared and inherited across the organization. Models For us, it is about mapping intelligence to a given task, with the best economics. This is something we can uniquely do in the context of real-world tasks by tuning our products, harness and tools, and the model system, end-to-end. And today we are thrilled to announce Microsoft-Decision-1.1 , which is now generally available and ready for enterprise deployment. We have added multimodal support. And we have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster. Already, more than 4,000 customers have used it. And we ourselves are using it for core tasks like routing, data labeling, personalization, content filtering and hundreds of other use cases. Foundry of course has all the most popular closed and open weight models, too. We are very excited to bring GPT 6.2 to Foundry. It is a great model that sets a new bar for AI in professional work. And today we are announcing that Meta’s latest models are all coming to Foundry as well. We are also innovating at the frontier with our own MAI model family that is both compute-efficient when it comes to pre-training and token-efficient when it comes to product deployment. Our goal is to put additional points on the frontier curve informed by real world task-performance. And we are going further. We are announcing MAI Licensed Weights, meaning our trusted customers will now be able to get access to Microsoft AI model weights through our Frontier Co. Today, we are introducing lots of new models . But I want to highlight two in particular: First, Code. We are introducing our new flagship family of agentic coding models: Code 2. Code 2 is at the frontier of cost-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. It excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multifile implementation, repo-wide reasoning and UI at a fraction of frontier cost. Code 2 Flash is designed for fast, high-volume work like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes and rapid iterations. It brings near-flagship quality for a much lower cost. These models are both generally available today on GitHub Copilot, both in the model picker and as part of Copilot Fusion. They are also available in Foundry. We are taking the same approach in cyber. Cyber 2 Flash is our most capable security model yet. It is a flash-sized model that delivers performance ahead of frontier models at a fraction of the cost per task. And, just as we have done with coding, we are co-designing the model with the tools and systems where it will be used. We are integrating Cyber 2 with Perception. Agent 365 Successfully deploying AI systems starts with making sure you have observability at every layer of the stack. That is where Agent 365 comes in. It is a control plane that extends your existing governance, identity, security and management systems to the agents in your enterprise. We already have over 50 million agents in Agent 365. And it includes FinOps, too. As AI scales, every organization needs a clear line between what it spends and the value AI creates. That is why today we are announcing Agent 365 Business Analytics. You can think of it as your ERP system for AI usage. You can see exactly what is driving spend. You can connect spend to outcomes to drive business value. And you can optimize ROI across different scenarios. Security The next thing I want to talk about is how you take the environment you have set up, from Copilot to IQ to Agent 365, and secure it. And that is where Perception and our security stack comes in. We are building an end-to-end trust platform. We are helping customers both secure their AI deployments and use AI to strengthen their security posture. Perception is a complete agentic security system with teams of red, blue and green agents that run through playbooks to deliver security outcomes at machine speed, with you always in control. Essentially, think about it like this: red team agents simulate attacks, blue team agents detect attacks and green team agents fix and remediate. With Playbooks, you can compose teams of agents to tackle complex jobs and trigger them to take action autonomously. Perception helps connect all the signals, sensors and actuators across your identity, client, cloud, apps and agents to intelligence to secure your end-to-end environments. And I am very excited to share that Perception is now generally available. In addition to the work we have been doing across our products, we are also working across the ecosystem to ensure everyone can innovate at speed and scale, safely. Today, we can see almost everything models touch. But we cannot see what happens inside the model. And what the model tells us about itself is not independent evidence. These nested black boxes are simply unacceptable. We need to be able to examine what AI sees and does, verify its actions independently and control what it is allowed to do. That is why today we are also announcing the Microsoft AI Transparency Initiative . There are three parts to this: First, we will expand our collaboration in NIST’s Agent Standards Initiative, drawing on its research to help lead the development of open, industry-wide standards for AI transparency, security and governance. Second, we are taking a full ecosystem approach. Together, we can enable AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider. Already, 40 organizations are working with us on defining and applying these standards. Third, we are working to incorporate the same standards in our products, including MAI models, Foundry and Copilot. Our ambition through our research, our product work and our ecosystem is to help establish an open industry standard that makes AI safer, more transparent and more accessible. Cobalt 200 VMs Underneath all of this is unbelievable silicon. We are building a heterogeneous platform working across the ecosystem to bring you all the latest innovation. We are also advancing our own hardware systems, co-designing silicon, servers and infrastructure to get more from every watt, chip and datacenter. We just announced Maia 300, which will deliver 40 percent more tokens per watt compared with leading GPU-based systems. Azure Boost and Azure Integrated HSM move critical infrastructure and security functions into purpose-built silicon. And today we are announcing general availability of our next-generation Cobalt 200 VMs , which are our highest-performing general-purpose VMs with leading price-performance. So, that is a quick walk through some of our news. When you look at all that is coming, it is clear that we are entering an era of ubiquitous intelligence. The key imperatives for us are to ensure human ambition, a firm’s control of its own intelligence and the diffusion of the benefits broadly. That is the promise of a frontier ecosystem. And that is what we are here to build together. For more information on today’s announcements, check out the Book of News . title: Four Continents, Four New AWS Heroes: Closing Out 2026
body: Four Continents, Four New AWS Heroes: Closing Out 2026 As AWS re:Invent is around the corner, we’re proud to recognize a new group of AWS Heroes . Every Hero finds their own way to give back, whether through sharing what they know, bringing people together, or building tools that help others succeed. What they have in common is a genuine commitment to supporting the builders around them learn, grow, and lead. Let us take a moment to meet them! Andres Moreno – El Paso, United States Serverless Hero Andres Moreno leads the Cloud del Norte AWS User Group and is a former AWS Community Builder. On his blog, And More Dev, and at conferences and community events, he explains serverless, cloud native architectures, generative AI, and agentic systems in ways that make new technology easier to try. Andres puts special energy into supporting builders across Latin America and helping them explore what’s possible on AWS. Geethika Guruge – Auckland, New Zealand Community Hero Geethika Guruge is a Principal Consultant at Mantel Group whose work spans serverless, DevOps, cloud infrastructure, and agentic AI. Geethika has shared real lessons from building agentic applications and leading large migration and modernization programs at AWS re:Invent, AWS Summits, and AWS Community Days. At home in Auckland, Geethika organizes local AWS meetups that encourage grassroots innovation and mentors the next generation of cloud architects and leaders. Jéssica Cristina Coelho – Belo Horizonte, Brazil Data Hero Jéssica Cristina Coelho is a Database Reliability Engineer and a former AWS Community Builder with more than 15 years of experience in databases, cloud, and data engineering. She leads the AWS User Group in Minas Gerais, hosts DataTalks Brasil, teaches MBA courses, and supports Women in Cloud, DevOpsDays, and AWS Community Day events. She speaks at events such as AWS Summit São Paulo and Web Summit Rio on database modernization and generative AI. At AWS re:Invent 2025, she was recognized as a LATAM Diversity & Inclusion Champion. Kazuho Cryer Shinozuka – Tokyo, Japan DevTools Hero Kazuho Cryer Shinozuka is an AWS CDK Top Contributor and Trusted CDK Community Reviewer. With 200 merged pull requests, he ranks 18th among more than 1,700 contributors. He has reviewed more than 120 pull requests, has been involved in about 2% of all CDK commits, and has published 10 construct libraries, along with tools such as cfn idle cost. Through talks at JAWS DAYS and CDK Conference Japan and through hands on contribution workshops, he helps more developers in Japan start contributing to open source. Learn More To connect with these Heroes or find one in your region, explore the AWS Heroes webpage , and join the conversation on AWS Builder Center . — Taylor

title: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents
body: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents At SC26, NVIDIA’s VP of Hyperscale and HPC laid out how researchers can combine simulation, AI and agents to accelerate scientific discovery. November 17, 2026 by Brian Caulfield 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. Open Models for Science Agents “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. Researchers can run it locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation or their own supercomputer. At Argonne National Laboratory, Buck said, an agent built with the toolkit took a single prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, chose which simulations to run and identified two new binding sites. “You own your data. You own the model,” Buck said. Buck highlighted other agents already in use: GROMACS: An agent from KTH Royal Institute of Technology repairs broken GROMACS setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single DGX Spark, it fixed 81% of test cases. SETI Institute: At the Allen Telescope Array, an agent took a one-line prompt to plot a methanol line. Buck explained that it then retuned for Doppler shift on its own [NGC 869 vs. 896, check slide]. Nsight AI Porting Agent: NVIDIA’s new agent ported a routine from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to GPUs, Buck said, speeding it up more than 5x using about 150 million tokens. CPUs for the Agent Loop Agents lean on CPUs to run tool calls between model steps, Buck explained. “That’s exactly what agents need,” he said. “They need a CPU that can run, evaluate, run the tool, perform the operations, gather the results.” DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer, expected in early 2028. Buck said it joins Vera systems already announced at Texas Advanced Computing Center. A New GPU for Science Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the Vera Rubin platform, built for science, engineering, analytics and AI, Buck said. It supports precisions from FP64 to FP4, adds sparse-data acceleration and connects over seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink. With more than 50,000 CUDA cores, it has about three times as many as Hopper, Buck said. It is expected in 2028. Quantum Error Correction Buck said a simulation on Jülich’s JUPITER supercomputer showed that a technique called magic state cultivation can cut the operations needed for one logical step tenfold. The work is being added to CUDA-Q. NVIDIA, IBM and Fermilab announced plans today for a quantum computing co-design platform to support error-correction and applications research. NVIDIA and IBM are pairing NVIDIA DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk. Buck also introduced a new breakthrough for quantum decoding. The goal, Buck explained, is to cut decoding latency from about 300 microseconds to 10. A new CUDA-Q decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, cuts error-correction research computation from 12 weeks to 45 minutes, he said. Networking Buck also showed one of the first deployments of NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics switches, at Lambda . He said they are 15x more reliable on bit errors and link flaps. See notice regarding software product information. Mia Nagawiecki and Chance Coughenour are celebrating 100 years of Colonial Williamsburg by bringing its history to your screen. You can now explore thousands of newly digitized manuscripts, rare archival photos, and interactive galleries from home. These collections highlight the lives of ordinary people and the work behind preserving early American history. You can visit the Google Arts & Culture website to view these treasures, read new stories, and learn about 18th-century traditions. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Today, as Colonial Williamsburg marks its 100th anniversary, Google Arts & Culture is sharing new immersive stories and newly digitized cultural artifacts that honor a century of preservation, discovery, and public access. These additions expand on the digital hub we launched earlier this year with The Colonial Williamsburg Foundation to celebrate America’s 250th birthday and bring the rich history of early America online. Discover the latest stories and archives We’re introducing three new ways to explore Colonial Williamsburg’s legendary collections, taking you behind the scenes of how history is preserved, studied, and brought to life. Step inside an immersive online gallery : Learn about the Historic Area’s restoration, which began in 1926. This interactive gallery pairs rare archival photos with modern photography and period music across the first three reconstructed sites: the Governor’s Palace , the Raleigh Tavern , and the Capitol. Browse more than 3,000 new digital records : Through our ongoing collaboration, a specialized high-resolution tabletop scanner has helped digitize tightly bound volumes, delicate manuscripts, and centuries-old records. Today, we’re launching over 3,000 newly scanned images — including rare issues of the Virginia Gazette , fragile archival records, and special collections assets — making many of these treasures accessible to the public online for the very first time. Read new stories celebrating 100 years : New immersive stories capture the breadth of Colonial Williamsburg’s work and collections. Ranging from rare natural history surveys and early newspapers to reproductions and everyday items , these narratives explore the complex tapestry of American history through the experiences of ordinary people and the vital legacies of historically marginalized voices — and showcase the behind-the-scenes work keeping their histories alive. Explore newly digitized plates from naturalist Mark Catesby’s 18th-century masterwork, bringing 220 hand-engraved illustrations of North American wildlife and flora into brilliant, high resolution. Step inside the new online gallery to see the restoration of Colonial Williamsburg, spotlighting its first three reconstructed sites: the Governor's Palace, the Raleigh Tavern, and the Capitol. Dive into vivid watercolor and ink pages from folk artist Lewis Miller’s 19th-century sketchbook, offering a rare and powerful window into everyday Virginia life and the domestic slave trade. Discover historic American transportation through a rare folio of carriage drawings, showcasing the visual diversity of Colonial Williamsburg's library collections. Uncover the story of “Authentic Colors from Colonial Williamsburg” — a rare book featuring metal pages coated in historic automotive paints inspired by Colonial Williamsburg — and its unique conservation journey. Step into the kitchen with Max Miller’s “Tasting History” In partnership with Colonial Williamsburg and YouTube, culinary historian Max Miller, creator of “Tasting History,” visited the living history museum to film an exclusive episode , bringing 18th-century traditions to life. Praising the museum’s meticulous historical accuracy, Miller worked alongside Ivey Boyd, chef de cuisine at the King’s Arms Tavern, to prepare snow eggs ( oeufs à la neige ). This French dessert was popularized in early America by James Hemings, Thomas Jefferson's enslaved chef, and is served today at Colonial Williamsburg. This collaboration bridges traditional preservation with modern storytelling, inviting a new generation to discover the flavors and stories of early America. Look ahead to the next century of access By expanding access to Colonial Williamsburg’s collections, we’re safeguarding centuries-old treasures while sharing their history with the world. As Colonial Williamsburg enters its second century, we invite you to experience these new stories, archival records, and the living history of early America in a whole new way. title: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab
body: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab November 16, 2026 by Allen Bourgoyne 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems , each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. A Supercomputing Lab on Any Desk The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 16TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1. With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises. The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems. The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures. Running on DGX Spark, new open dataset and post-training recipes for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL help researchers adapt the model for life sciences and chemistry, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control. What Researchers Can Do With It The kit opens up new possibilities for researchers. Researchers can explore agent-assisted workflows that prepare simulation inputs, launch runs and summarize results, while the scientists validate the setup and conclusions. Researchers can also train AI models that approximate slow simulations, then use them to refine wing designs toward minimum drag. Before committing supercomputer time, a team can narrow a 10-million-cell simulation to the 50-500 dimensions that matter. Kvantify is using NVIDIA cuQuantum, and reports running tensor-network simulations of quantum-chemistry circuits with up to 70 qubits and 975 gates on a single DGX Spark, benchmarking circuits generated for penicillin ground-state energy calculations. CYRAN AI , an IIT Delhi spin-out, uses DGX Spark and its PixelFlux library to accelerate JPEG 2000 decoding for large satellite images, supporting local geospatial analysis. OpenFold shows how researchers can fine-tune OpenFold3 on NVIDIA DGX Spark to improve protein-ligand structure predictions for drug discovery. The Rubin Lab at IGI at University of California, Berkeley is using a DGX Spark and NVIDIA Evo 2 model to predict bacterial traits directly from genome sequences by comparing embeddings from genomic and protein language models against the classical baselines. With no 11-hour cluster queue times, results arrived 15x sooner on DGX Spark. The Hartwig Group at UC Berkeley is using a DGX Spark to perform LoRA fine-tuning on the Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B model for chemistry machine learning, training a prediction head on experimental values. By running locally on the Spark using NVFP4 quantization, the lab successfully fit a 120B-class model on a single device and bypassed multi-day cluster queue times, allowing them to run continuous eight- to 24-hour training fits back-to-back. Where to Find the Kit The developer kit is on display at SC26 and available for sale. DGX Spark products and cables can be purchased from top OEM partners and are also available through NVIDIA Marketplace . Partners include Acer, ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, H3C, HP, Lenovo, MSI and xFusion. An NVIDIA playbook for building and running the NVIDIA HPC SDK, a software development kit for scientific computing, is coming soon. Once available, it will give scientists and researchers a local platform to develop multi-node GPU applications, explore FP32 and mixed-precision algorithms and run molecular dynamics and materials simulations using LAMMPS with Kokkos before scaling to data center systems. Learn more about NVIDIA DGX Spark . Subscribe to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter . Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X , Instagram , TikTok and Facebook . See notice regarding software product information. title: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future
body: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future Over two decades running the most complex manufacturing on the planet, NVIDIA operations chief Deb Shoquist has required three things of every supply chain partner: extreme technical skill, unshakeable trust and a willingness to always try something new. November 16, 2026 by NVIDIA Writers 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades. Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round. Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago. For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it. Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow. Shoquist meets with key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year on the road visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors. Recently, she paused her travels to accept the 2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award — and to share how she finds the right people and companies to imagine and produce at massive scale technology that has never been built before. Foxconn Q: How would you describe your job to someone outside NVIDIA? A: At the most basic level, our job is to convert designs into the physical world. Our design team creates a blueprint, and our job is to transition it into a reliable, high-performance supply chain. A matchmaker is probably the best analogy. You have to find the partner that matches your ramp style and has the technology that can meet the needs of very precise designs. The supplier has to be financially strong enough to invest in our ramps. They have to be highly technical. And they have to be willing to do something that has never been done before. If you don’t have all three, you can’t create products at the volume and speed that we need. You need those three legs, and in some cases, if you only have two, you have to invest in the company to make them a partner. Q: What’s an example of that in practice ? A: Amphenol’s cable cartridge is the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. When I recently visited the Vietnam factory, now in full production, I was struck by the level of precision required to build a product of this complexity. In this large cable cartridge, there are 1,500 small cable legs. Each one requires a very precise assembly to yield a quality level of less than 1 DPPM, or defect part per million. Amphenol built over a hundred automated lines to produce this product at the speed and scale we require. That takes know-how and technology, but it also takes heart, willingness and dedication. Creating anything of that complexity and precision with a supplier forges the partnership. The partners NVIDIA maintains are the ones who supported us when we were small, and yet are willing to scale with us today. Q: What changed as NVIDIA went from selling chips to building systems and platforms? A: When we were primarily a chip manufacturer, we were small, and the semiconductor industry was at scale. In that environment, it was about picking the best technology match for the products we envisioned. As we became a data center systems company, we needed more partners. But we’ve also now entered into new technology areas where the scale of the supply base is still developing. For example, our optical component partners have the technology and the willingness, but they don’t yet have the scale or capital to build fabs for the volume we need. To grow, we needed to support and invest, like we did with Coherent and Lumentum . Beyond that, with products like CPO (co-packaged optics), we’re creating entirely new supply chains with scale partners that are new to the optics world. Leading the integration of talent across the supply chain is the key to driving this incredible technology to high volume quickly. Wistron Q: You clearly enjoy spending time with supply partners, and in particular on the factory floor. What have you learned there over time that can’t be learned anywhere else? A: Over 20 years, you meet many individuals key to the success of your supply. You meet not only the CEOs, but also the people that are running the production floor. These are the people that really know the problems of manufacturing. If you don’t have a tight working relationship with the people deeper in the organization, then it’s hard to have an open dialogue about any challenges. But when you have tight relationships, they want to help you, and they feel comfortable enough telling you, “I need better technical support on the floor. I need more quality engineers. We need a better design. We need to automate this. We need more buffers of material.” That’s what 20 years of working with our suppliers has taught us. It’s year after year of learning from people, getting to know people deeper in the organization and creating the trust where they can tell us what we need to do to be successful with them. Q: Demand for NVIDIA technology is already massive and growing. Your job is to make sure NVIDIA’s volume can keep up. How do you make it happen? A: It goes back to relationships. When you decide that you’re going to push a line hard to increase volume, you have to have the relationships. You have to know their processes in detail. You have to know their people in detail, and they have to trust you. Only then are you in a position to ask them for special favors, because you can do it surgically, and your ask is credible and reasonable. And when you’re successful together, they’re happy, you’re happy, and the appreciation for the partnership deepens. We all appreciate those that make us successful. Coherent Q: How do you prioritize resources across the supply chain? A: You need to first understand what the most critical components are, and protect and prioritize production around them. We need wafers like we need air. And the critical component is the TSMC chip. As it comes out of assembly every week, we decide what factory gets what chip. Every week, we look at factory performance. If a particular factory yield is low, if their time of ownership is not at the level we want, they don’t get more chips that week. We keep track of every chip, from the identification number on the die all the way to the customer invoice. If you want to be our supplier, you have to support that traceability process. With that process, we took the time it takes from chip out at TSMC to system out at Foxconn and Wistron from five to two weeks when supply and demand requires it. Think of the supply chain as a large circulatory system with pathways everywhere — and when you need to accelerate any branch of it, you have the power to do that. We have the capability to do that. It’s empowering and exciting. Amphenol Q: What’s an example of a time things didn’t go as planned? How did you, the team and your partners find a way forward? A: We were getting ready to go to volume production with Foxconn and Wistron for the compute board of NVIDIA GB200 . The last step in the process was a test managed by an automated handler — a completely new approach for us, developed to meet the demands of high-volume throughput for these complicated products. During the initial ramp, the throughput was significantly below plan. The operations director of Taiwan manufacturing made the call that to protect the product and shipments, he needed to disable the entire process and return to manual test loading. Our manufacturers backed him without question and brought in the necessary manpower to meet the immediate needs, literally hundreds of operators. That kept production moving, but would not solve the throughput requirement of full production. As with any operations problem, the root cause had many elements to it: test tray assembly, test tray design, automation hardware design, automation control software, product yield. From all viewpoints, it was a difficult problem to resolve quickly. That’s when we executed the NVIDIA swarm. Teams from NVIDIA design engineering, operations industrial, and product and test engineering, as well as from Foxconn automation engineering, flooded the line with talent to redesign and reactivate the line before the scale ramp hit. This is not an unusual occurrence when there is a problem in operations. All teams at NVIDIA are street fighters — action-oriented, and know no organizational boundaries. We say that “the mission is the boss,” but we also live “the mission is the boss.” Q: What makes this work so exciting for you? A: Operations is a very empowering place to be at NVIDIA. Our team is designing and implementing changes to the supply chain constantly to meet the strong demand of our new products. The challenges are understandably high, but we’re always given the resources we need to be successful. The only thing between our goals and our success is our own creativity. That is exhilarating. retained_feed_body: Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades. Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round. Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago. For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it. Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow. Shoquist meets with key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year on the road visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors. Recently, she paused her travels to accept the 2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award — and to share how she finds the right people and companies to imagine and produce at massive scale technology that has never been built before. Foxconn Q: How would you describe your job to someone outside NVIDIA? A: At the most basic level, our job is to convert designs into the physical world. Our design team creates a blueprint, and our job is to transition it into a reliable, high-performance supply chain. A matchmaker is probably the best analogy. You have to find the partner that matches your ramp style and has the technology that can meet the needs of very precise designs. The supplier has to be financially strong enough to invest in our ramps. They have to be highly technical. And they have to be willing to do something that has never been done before. If you don’t have all three, you can’t create products at the volume and speed that we need. You need those three legs, and in some cases, if you only have two, you have to invest in the company to make them a partner. Q: What’s an example of that in practice ? A: Amphenol’s cable cartridge is the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. When I recently visited the Vietnam factory, now in full production, I was struck by the level of precision required to build a product of this complexity. In this large cable cartridge, there are 1,500 small cable legs. Each one requires a very precise assembly to yield a quality level of less than 1 DPPM, or defect part per million. Amphenol built over a hundred automated lines to produce this product at the speed and scale we require. That takes know-how and technology, but it also takes heart, willingness and dedication. Creating anything of that complexity and precision with a supplier forges the partnership. The partners NVIDIA maintains are the ones who supported us when we were small, and yet are willing to scale with us today. Q: What changed as NVIDIA went from selling chips to building systems and platforms? A: When we were primarily a chip manufacturer, we were small, and the semiconductor industry was at scale. In that environment, it was about picking the best technology match for the products we envisioned. As we became a data center systems company, we needed more partners. But we’ve also now entered into new technology areas where the scale of the supply base is still developing. For example, our optical component partners have the technology and the willingness, but they don’t yet have the scale or capital to build fabs for the volume we need. To grow, we needed to support and invest, like we did with Coherent and Lumentum . Beyond that, with products like CPO (co-packaged optics), we’re creating entirely new supply chains with scale partners that are new to the optics world. Leading the integration of talent across the supply chain is the key to driving this incredible technology to high volume quickly. Wistron Q: You clearly enjoy spending time with supply partners, and in particular on the factory floor. What have you learned there over time that can’t be learned anywhere else? A: Over 20 years, you meet many individuals key to the success of your supply. You meet not only the CEOs, but also the people that are running the production floor. These are the people that really know the problems of manufacturing. If you don’t have a tight working relationship with the people deeper in the organization, then it’s hard to have an open dialogue about any challenges. But when you have tight relationships, they want to help you, and they feel comfortable enough telling you, “I need better technical support on the floor. I need more quality engineers. We need a better design. We need to automate this. We need more buffers of material.” That’s what 20 years of working with our suppliers has taught us. It’s year after year of learning from people, getting to know people deeper in the organization and creating the trust where they can tell us what we need to do to be successful with them. Q: Demand for NVIDIA technology is already massive and growing. Your job is to make sure NVIDIA’s volume can keep up. How do you make it happen? A: It goes back to relationships. When you decide that you’re going to push a line hard to increase volume, you have to have the relationships. You have to know their processes in detail. You have to know their people in detail, and they have to trust you. Only then are you in a position to ask them for special favors, because you can do it surgically, and your ask is credible and reasonable. And when you’re successful together, they’re happy, you’re happy, and the appreciation for the partnership deepens. We all appreciate those that make us successful. Coherent Q: How do you prioritize resources across the supply chain? A: You need to first understand what the most critical components are, and protect and prioritize production around them. We need wafers like we need air. And the critical component is the TSMC chip. As it comes out of assembly every week, we decide what factory gets what chip. Every week, we look at factory performance. If a particular factory yield is low, if their time of ownership is not at the level we want, they don’t get more chips that week. We keep track of every chip, from the identification number on the die all the way to the customer invoice. If you want to be our supplier, you have to support that traceability process. With that process, we took the time it takes from chip out at TSMC to system out at Foxconn and Wistron from five to two weeks when supply and demand requires it. Think of the supply chain as a large circulatory system with pathways everywhere — and when you need to accelerate any branch of it, you have the power to do that. We have the capability to do that. It’s empowering and exciting. Amphenol Q: What’s an example of a time things didn’t go as planned? How did you, the team and your partners find a way forward? A: We were getting ready to go to volume production with Foxconn and Wistron for the compute board of NVIDIA GB200 . The last step in the process was a test managed by an automated handler — a completely new approach for us, developed to meet the demands of high-volume throughput for these complicated products. During the initial ramp, the throughput was significantly below plan. The operations director of Taiwan manufacturing made the call that to protect the product and shipments, he needed to disable the entire process and return to manual test loading. Our manufacturers backed him without question and brought in the necessary manpower to meet the immediate needs, literally hundreds of operators. title: AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Nitro Sandboxes, AWS Emulator, and more (November 16, 2026)
body: AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Nitro Sandboxes, AWS Emulator, and more (November 16, 2026) A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt. I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also new ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS . Headlines Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough shows a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub . What I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production. AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs . You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: Amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito . The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus plans in all Cognito Regions. Claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements : Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use. Amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. Amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges. Amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch , with policies covering existing groups or only new ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE). The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – New Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock – This guide follows an agent’s cost through repeated calls, reasoning, caching, and human review. I like its emphasis on measuring a completed task and comparing outcomes against a documented baseline. Its worked prices are illustrative; use your own workload and reconcile estimated costs with billing data. How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions – Zillow describes reusable content modules and configuration-driven AWS Step Functions Express Workflows for more than 100 million daily notifications. The useful engineering details include idempotent modules, batching, campaign isolation, and testing expressions with the TestState API before deployment. Those patterns apply well beyond notification systems. Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events: AWS re:Invent – Join the community in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. Browse more than 2,200 sessions, including workshops and deep dives, or register for the free livestream to follow keynotes and selected sessions remotely. AWS Community Days – Find community-led technical talks, workshops, and hands-on learning near you. Check each organizer’s page for current dates and registration details. Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup! – Daniel Abib This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!
